# memchr - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/memchr/

## Expand description

This library provides heavily optimized routines for string search primitives.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

This section gives a brief high level overview of what this crate offers.

- The top-level module provides routines for searching for 1, 2 or 3 bytes in the forward or reverse direction. When searching for more than one byte, positions are considered a match if the byte at that position matches any of the bytes.
- The `memmem`

In all such cases, routines operate on `&[u8]` without regard to encoding. This
is exactly what you want when searching either UTF-8 or arbitrary bytes.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-using-memchr)Example: using `memchr`

This example shows how to use `memchr` to find the first occurrence of `z` in
a haystack:

```
use memchr::memchr;
let haystack = b"foo bar baz quuz";
assert_eq!(Some(10), memchr(b'z', haystack));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-matching-one-of-three-possible-bytes)Example: matching one of three possible bytes

This examples shows how to use `memrchr3` to find occurrences of `a`, `b` or
`c`, starting at the end of the haystack.

```
use memchr::memchr3_iter;
let haystack = b"xyzaxyzbxyzc";
let mut it = memchr3_iter(b'a', b'b', b'c', haystack).rev();
assert_eq!(Some(11), it.next());
assert_eq!(Some(7), it.next());
assert_eq!(Some(3), it.next());
assert_eq!(None, it.next());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-iterating-over-substring-matches)Example: iterating over substring matches

This example shows how to use the [ memmem](https://docs.rs/memmem/index.html) sub-module to find occurrences of
a substring in a haystack.

```
use memchr::memmem;
let haystack = b"foo bar foo baz foo";
let mut it = memmem::find_iter(haystack, "foo");
assert_eq!(Some(0), it.next());
assert_eq!(Some(8), it.next());
assert_eq!(Some(16), it.next());
assert_eq!(None, it.next());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example-repeating-a-search-for-the-same-needle)Example: repeating a search for the same needle

It may be possible for the overhead of constructing a substring searcher to be
measurable in some workloads. In cases where the same needle is used to search
many haystacks, it is possible to do construction once and thus to avoid it for
subsequent searches. This can be done with a [ memmem::Finder](https://docs.rs/memmem/struct.Finder.html):

```
use memchr::memmem;
let finder = memmem::Finder::new("foo");
assert_eq!(Some(4), finder.find(b"baz foo quux"));
assert_eq!(None, finder.find(b"quux baz bar"));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#why-use-this-crate)Why use this crate?

At first glance, the APIs provided by this crate might seem weird. Why provide
a dedicated routine like `memchr` for something that could be implemented
clearly and trivially in one line:

```
fn memchr(needle: u8, haystack: &[u8]) -> Option<usize> {
    haystack.iter().position(|&b| b == needle)
}
```
Or similarly, why does this crate provide substring search routines when Rust’s core library already provides them?

```
fn search(haystack: &str, needle: &str) -> Option<usize> {
    haystack.find(needle)
}
```
The primary reason for both of them to exist is performance. When it comes to performance, at a high level at least, there are two primary ways to look at it:

- **Throughput**: For this, think about it as, “given some very large haystack and a byte that never occurs in that haystack, how long does it take to search through it and determine that it, in fact, does not occur?”
- **Latency**: For this, think about it as, “given a tiny haystack—just a few bytes—how long does it take to determine if a byte is in it?”

The `memchr` routine in this crate has *slightly* worse latency than the
solution presented above, however, its throughput can easily be over an
order of magnitude faster. This is a good general purpose trade off to make.
You rarely lose, but often gain big.

**NOTE:** The name `memchr` comes from the corresponding routine in `libc`. A
key advantage of using this library is that its performance is not tied to its
quality of implementation in the `libc` you happen to be using, which can vary
greatly from platform to platform.

But what about substring search? This one is a bit more complicated. The primary reason for its existence is still indeed performance, but it’s also useful because Rust’s core library doesn’t actually expose any substring search routine on arbitrary bytes. The only substring search routine that exists works exclusively on valid UTF-8.

So if you have valid UTF-8, is there a reason to use this over the standard library substring search routine? Yes. This routine is faster on almost every metric, including latency. The natural question then, is why isn’t this implementation in the standard library, even if only for searching on UTF-8? The reason is that the implementation details for using SIMD in the standard library haven’t quite been worked out yet.

**NOTE:** Currently, only `x86_64`, `wasm32` and `aarch64` targets have vector
accelerated implementations of `memchr` (and friends) and `memmem`.

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate features

- **std**- When enabled (the default), this will permit features specific to the standard library. Currently, the only thing used from the standard library is runtime SIMD CPU feature detection. This means that this feature must be enabled to get AVX2 accelerated routines on- `x86_64`targets without enabling the- `avx2`feature at compile time, for example. When- `std`is not enabled, this crate will still attempt to use SSE2 accelerated routines on- `x86_64`. It will also use AVX2 accelerated routines when the- `avx2`feature is enabled at compile time. In general, enable this feature if you can.
- **alloc**- When enabled (the default), APIs in this crate requiring some kind of allocation will become available. For example, the- `memmem::Finder::into_owned`- `arch::all::shiftor`- `alloc`feature doesn’t add much currently. Notably, disabling- `std`but enabling- `alloc`will- **not**result in the use of AVX2 on- `x86_64`targets unless the- `avx2`feature is enabled at compile time. (With- `std`enabled, AVX2 can be used even without the- `avx2`feature enabled at compile time by way of runtime CPU feature detection.)
- **logging**- When enabled (disabled by default), the- `log`crate is used to emit log messages about what kinds of- `memchr`and- `memmem`algorithms are used. Namely, both- `memchr`and- `memmem`have a number of different implementation choices depending on the target and CPU, and the log messages can help show what specific implementations are being used. Generally, this is useful for debugging performance issues.
- **libc**-- **DEPRECATED**. Previously, this enabled the use of the target’s- `memchr`function from whatever- `libc`was linked into the program. This feature is now a no-op because this crate’s implementation of- `memchr`should now be sufficiently fast on a number of platforms that- `libc`should no longer be needed. (This feature is somewhat of a holdover from this crate’s origins. Originally, this crate was literally just a safe wrapper function around the- `memchr`function from- `libc`.)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [arch](https://docs.rs/arch/index.html)
- A module with low-level architecture dependent routines.
- [memmem](https://docs.rs/memmem/index.html)
- This module provides forward and reverse substring search routines.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Memchr](https://docs.rs/struct.Memchr.html)
- An iterator over all occurrences of a single byte in a haystack.
- [Memchr2](https://docs.rs/struct.Memchr2.html)
- An iterator over all occurrences of two possible bytes in a haystack.
- [Memchr3](https://docs.rs/struct.Memchr3.html)
- An iterator over all occurrences of three possible bytes in a haystack.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [memchr](https://docs.rs/fn.memchr.html)
- Search for the first occurrence of a byte in a slice.
- [memchr2](https://docs.rs/fn.memchr2.html)
- Search for the first occurrence of two possible bytes in a haystack.
- [memchr3](https://docs.rs/fn.memchr3.html)
- Search for the first occurrence of three possible bytes in a haystack.
- [memchr2_](https://docs.rs/fn.memchr2_iter.html)- iter
- Returns an iterator over all occurrences of the needles in a haystack.
- [memchr3_](https://docs.rs/fn.memchr3_iter.html)- iter
- Returns an iterator over all occurrences of the needles in a haystack.
- [memchr_](https://docs.rs/fn.memchr_iter.html)- iter
- Returns an iterator over all occurrences of the needle in a haystack.
- [memrchr](https://docs.rs/fn.memrchr.html)
- Search for the last occurrence of a byte in a slice.
- [memrchr2](https://docs.rs/fn.memrchr2.html)
- Search for the last occurrence of two possible bytes in a haystack.
- [memrchr3](https://docs.rs/fn.memrchr3.html)
- Search for the last occurrence of three possible bytes in a haystack.
- [memrchr2_](https://docs.rs/fn.memrchr2_iter.html)- iter
- Returns an iterator over all occurrences of the needles in a haystack, in reverse.
- [memrchr3_](https://docs.rs/fn.memrchr3_iter.html)- iter
- Returns an iterator over all occurrences of the needles in a haystack, in reverse.
- [memrchr_](https://docs.rs/fn.memrchr_iter.html)- iter
- Returns an iterator over all occurrences of the needle in a haystack, in reverse.

# memchr 2.8.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/memchr/latest

# memchr

This library provides heavily optimized routines for string search primitives.

Dual-licensed under MIT or the [UNLICENSE](https://unlicense.org/).

### Documentation

### Overview

- The top-level module provides routines for searching for 1, 2 or 3 bytes in the forward or reverse direction. When searching for more than one byte, positions are considered a match if the byte at that position matches any of the bytes.
- The `memmem`sub-module provides forward and reverse substring search routines.

In all such cases, routines operate on `&[u8]` without regard to encoding. This
is exactly what you want when searching either UTF-8 or arbitrary bytes.

### Compiling without the standard library

memchr links to the standard library by default, but you can disable the
`std` feature if you want to use it in a `#![no_std]` crate:

```
[]
 = {  = "2",  = false }
```
On `x86_64` platforms, when the `std` feature is disabled, the SSE2 accelerated
implementations will be used. When `std` is enabled, AVX2 accelerated
implementations will be used if the CPU is determined to support it at runtime.

SIMD accelerated routines are also available on the `wasm32` and `aarch64`
targets. The `std` feature is not required to use them.

When a SIMD version is not available, then this crate falls back to
[SWAR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SWAR) techniques.

### Minimum Rust version policy

This crate's minimum supported `rustc` version is `1.61.0`.

The current policy is that the minimum Rust version required to use this crate
can be increased in minor version updates. For example, if `crate 1.0` requires
Rust 1.20.0, then `crate 1.0.z` for all values of `z` will also require Rust
1.20.0 or newer. However, `crate 1.y` for `y > 0` may require a newer minimum
version of Rust.

In general, this crate will be conservative with respect to the minimum supported version of Rust.

### Testing strategy

Given the complexity of the code in this crate, along with the pervasive use
of `unsafe`, this crate has an extensive testing strategy. It combines multiple
approaches:

- Hand-written tests.
- Exhaustive-style testing meant to exercise all possible branching and offset calculations.
- Property based testing through `quickcheck`
- Fuzz testing through `cargo fuzz`
- A huge suite of benchmarks that are also run as tests. Benchmarks always confirm that the expected result occurs.

Improvements to the testing infrastructure are very welcome.

### Algorithms used

At time of writing, this crate's implementation of substring search actually has a few different algorithms to choose from depending on the situation.

- For very small haystacks,
[Rabin-Karp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rabin%E2%80%93Karp_algorithm)is used to reduce latency. Rabin-Karp has very small overhead and can often complete before other searchers have even been constructed.
- For small needles, a variant of the
["Generic SIMD"](http://0x80.pl/articles/simd-strfind.html#algorithm-1-generic-simd)algorithm is used. Instead of using the first and last bytes, a heuristic is used to select bytes based on a background distribution of byte frequencies.
- In all other cases,
[Two-Way](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-way_string-matching_algorithm)is used. If possible, a prefilter based on the "Generic SIMD" algorithm linked above is used to find candidates quickly. A dynamic heuristic is used to detect if the prefilter is ineffective, and if so, disables it.

### Why is the standard library's substring search so much slower?

We'll start by establishing what the difference in performance actually
is. There are two relevant benchmark classes to consider: `prebuilt` and
`oneshot`. The `prebuilt` benchmarks are designed to measure---to the extent
possible---search time only. That is, the benchmark first starts by building a
searcher and then only tracking the time for *using* the searcher:

```
$ rebar rank benchmarks/record/x86_64/2023-08-26.csv --intersection -e memchr/memmem/prebuilt -e std/memmem/prebuilt
Engine                       Version                   Geometric mean of speed ratios  Benchmark count
------                       -------                   ------------------------------  ---------------
rust/memchr/memmem/prebuilt  2.5.0                     1.03                            53
rust/std/memmem/prebuilt     1.73.0-nightly 180dffba1  6.50                            53
```
Conversely, the `oneshot` benchmark class measures the time it takes to both
build the searcher *and* use it:

```
$ rebar rank benchmarks/record/x86_64/2023-08-26.csv --intersection -e memchr/memmem/oneshot -e std/memmem/oneshot
Engine                      Version                   Geometric mean of speed ratios  Benchmark count
------                      -------                   ------------------------------  ---------------
rust/memchr/memmem/oneshot  2.5.0                     1.04                            53
rust/std/memmem/oneshot     1.73.0-nightly 180dffba1  5.26                            53
```
**NOTE:** Replace `rebar rank` with `rebar cmp` in the above commands to
explore the specific benchmarks and their differences.

So in both cases, this crate is quite a bit faster over a broad sampling of benchmarks regardless of whether you measure only search time or search time plus construction time. The difference is a little smaller when you include construction time in your measurements.

These two different types of benchmark classes make for a nice segue into
one reason why the standard library's substring search can be slower: API
design. In the standard library, the only APIs available to you require
one to re-construct the searcher for every search. While you can benefit
from building a searcher once and iterating over all matches in a single
string, you cannot reuse that searcher to search other strings. This might
come up when, for example, searching a file one line at a time. You'll need
to re-build the searcher for every line searched, and this can [really
matter](https://blog.burntsushi.net/bstr/#motivation-based-on-performance).

**NOTE:** The `prebuilt` benchmark for the standard library can't actually
avoid measuring searcher construction at some level, because there is no API
for it. Instead, the benchmark consists of building the searcher once and then
finding all matches in a single string via an iterator. This tends to
approximate a benchmark where searcher construction isn't measured, but it
isn't perfect. While this means the comparison is not strictly
apples-to-apples, it does reflect what is maximally possible with the standard
library, and thus reflects the best that one could do in a real world scenario.

While there is more to the story than just API design here, it's important to
point out that even if the standard library's substring search were a precise
clone of this crate internally, it would still be at a disadvantage in some
workloads because of its API. (The same also applies to C's standard library
`memmem` function. There is no way to amortize construction of the searcher.
You need to pay for it on every call.)

The other reason for the difference in performance is that
the standard library has trouble using SIMD. In particular, substring search
is implemented in the `core` library, where platform specific code generally
can't exist. That's an issue because in order to utilize SIMD beyond SSE2
while maintaining portable binaries, one needs to use [dynamic CPU feature
detection](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/arch/index.html#dynamic-cpu-feature-detection), and that in turn requires platform specific code.
While there is [an RFC for enabling target feature detection in
 core](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3469), it doesn't yet exist.

The bottom line here is that `core`'s substring search implementation is
limited to making use of SSE2, but not AVX.

Still though, this crate does accelerate substring search even when only SSE2
is available. The standard library could therefore adopt the techniques in this
crate just for SSE2. The reason why that hasn't happened yet isn't totally
clear to me. It likely needs a champion to push it through. The standard
library tends to be more conservative in these things. With that said, the
standard library does use some [SSE2 acceleration on  x86-64](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/bf9229a2e366b4c311f059014a4aa08af16de5d8/library/core/src/str/pattern.rs#L1719-L1857) added
in

[this PR](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/103779). However, at the time of writing, it is only used for short needles and doesn't use the frequency based heuristics found in this crate.

**NOTE:** Another thing worth mentioning is that the standard library's
substring search routine requires that both the needle and haystack have type
`&str`. Unless you can assume that your data is valid UTF-8, building a `&str`
will come with the overhead of UTF-8 validation. This may in turn result in
overall slower searching depending on your workload. In contrast, the `memchr`
crate permits both the needle and the haystack to have type `&[u8]`, where
`&[u8]` can be created from a `&str` with zero cost. Therefore, the substring
search in this crate is strictly more flexible than what the standard library
provides.

---

# memchr 2.8.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/memchr/latest/source/

#
                    memchr 2.8.2

                Provides extremely fast (uses SIMD on x86_64, aarch64 and wasm32) routines for
1, 2 or 3 byte search and single substring search.

# log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/log/^0.4.20/

## Expand description

A lightweight logging facade.

The `log` crate provides a single logging API that abstracts over the
actual logging implementation. Libraries can use the logging API provided
by this crate, and the consumer of those libraries can choose the logging
implementation that is most suitable for its use case.

If no logging implementation is selected, the facade falls back to a “noop” implementation that ignores all log messages. The overhead in this case is very small - just an integer load, comparison and jump.

A log request consists of a *target*, a *level*, and a *body*. A target is a
string which defaults to the module path of the location of the log request,
though that default may be overridden. Logger implementations typically use
the target to filter requests based on some user configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The basic use of the log crate is through the five logging macros: [ error!](https://docs.rs/macro.error.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/macro.warn.html)

`warn!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.info.html)

`info!`[and](https://docs.rs/macro.debug.html)

`debug!`[where](https://docs.rs/macro.trace.html)

`trace!``error!` represents the highest-priority log messages
and `trace!` the lowest. The log messages are filtered by configuring
the log level to exclude messages with a lower priority.
Each of these macros accept format strings similarly to [.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/macro.println.html)

`println!`Avoid writing expressions with side-effects in log statements. They may not be evaluated.

[§](https://docs.rs#in-libraries)In libraries

Libraries should link only to the `log` crate, and use the provided
macros to log whatever information will be useful to downstream consumers.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", "Commencing yak shaving for {yak:?}");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!("Razor located: {razor}");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(err) => {
                warn!("Unable to locate a razor: {err}, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#in-executables)In executables

Executables should choose a logging implementation and initialize it early in the runtime of the program. Logging implementations will typically include a function to do this. Any log messages generated before the implementation is initialized will be ignored.

The executable itself may use the `log` crate to log as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

The logging system may only be initialized once.

[§](https://docs.rs#structured-logging)Structured logging

If you enable the `kv` feature you can associate structured values
with your log records. If we take the example from before, we can include
some additional context besides what’s in the formatted message:

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", yak:serde; "Commencing yak shaving");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!(razor; "Razor located");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(e) => {
                warn!(e:err; "Unable to locate a razor, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
See the [ kv](https://docs.rs/kv/index.html) module documentation for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#available-logging-implementations)Available logging implementations

In order to produce log output executables have to use a logger implementation compatible with the facade. There are many available implementations to choose from, here are some of the most popular ones:

- Simple minimal loggers:
- Complex configurable frameworks:
- Adaptors for other facilities:
- For WebAssembly binaries:
- For dynamic libraries:
- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over `log`to initialize in your libraries

- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over
- Utilities:

[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-a-logger)Implementing a Logger

Loggers implement the [ Log](https://docs.rs/trait.Log.html) trait. Here’s a very basic example that simply
logs all messages at the

[,](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Error`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Warn`[levels to stdout:](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Info````
use log::{Record, Level, Metadata};
struct SimpleLogger;
impl log::Log for SimpleLogger {
    fn enabled(&self, metadata: &Metadata) -> bool {
        metadata.level() <= Level::Info
    }
    fn log(&self, record: &Record) {
        if self.enabled(record.metadata()) {
            println!("{} - {}", record.level(), record.args());
        }
    }
    fn flush(&self) {}
}
```
Loggers are installed by calling the [ set_logger](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html) function. The maximum
log level also needs to be adjusted via the

[function. The logging facade uses this as an optimization to improve performance of log messages at levels that are disabled. It’s important to set it, as it defaults to](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level`[, so no log messages will ever be captured! In the case of our example logger, we’ll want to set the maximum log level to](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Off`[, since we ignore any](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Info`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Debug`[level log messages. A logging implementation should provide a function that wraps a call to](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Trace`[and](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html)

`set_logger`[, handling initialization of the logger:](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level````
use log::{SetLoggerError, LevelFilter};
static LOGGER: SimpleLogger = SimpleLogger;
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_logger(&LOGGER)
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
Implementations that adjust their configurations at runtime should take care to adjust the maximum log level as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-with-std)Use with `std`

`set_logger` requires you to provide a `&'static Log`, which can be hard to
obtain if your logger depends on some runtime configuration. The
`set_boxed_logger` function is available with the `std` Cargo feature. It is
identical to `set_logger` except that it takes a `Box<Log>` rather than a
`&'static Log`:

```
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_boxed_logger(Box::new(SimpleLogger))
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#compile-time-filters)Compile time filters

Log levels can be statically disabled at compile time by enabling one of these Cargo features:

- `max_level_off`
- `max_level_error`
- `max_level_warn`
- `max_level_info`
- `max_level_debug`
- `max_level_trace`

Log invocations at disabled levels will be skipped and will not even be present in the
resulting binary. These features control the value of the `STATIC_MAX_LEVEL` constant. The
logging macros check this value before logging a message. By default, no levels are disabled.

It is possible to override this level for release builds only with the following features:

- `release_max_level_off`
- `release_max_level_error`
- `release_max_level_warn`
- `release_max_level_info`
- `release_max_level_debug`
- `release_max_level_trace`

Libraries should avoid using the max level features because they’re global and can’t be changed once they’re set.

For example, a crate can disable trace level logs in debug builds and trace, debug, and info level logs in release builds with the following configuration:

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["max_level_debug", "release_max_level_warn"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags)Crate Feature Flags

The following crate feature flags are available in addition to the filters. They are
configured in your `Cargo.toml`.

- `std`allows use of- `std`crate instead of the default- `core`. Enables using- `std::error`and- `set_boxed_logger`functionality.
- `serde`enables support for serialization and deserialization of- `Level`and- `LevelFilter`.

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["std", "serde"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#version-compatibility)Version compatibility

The 0.3 and 0.4 versions of the `log` crate are almost entirely compatible. Log messages
made using `log` 0.3 will forward transparently to a logger implementation using `log` 0.4. Log
messages made using `log` 0.4 will forward to a logger implementation using `log` 0.3, but the
module path and file name information associated with the message will unfortunately be lost.

# quickcheck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quickcheck/^1.0.3/

## Expand description

This crate is a port of
[Haskell’s QuickCheck](https://hackage.haskell.org/package/QuickCheck).

QuickCheck is a library for random testing of program properties. The programmer provides a specification of the program, in the form of properties which functions should satisfy, and QuickCheck then tests that the properties hold in a large number of randomly generated cases.

For detailed examples, please see the
[README](https://github.com/BurntSushi/quickcheck).

[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

In general, this crate considers the `Arbitrary` implementations provided as
implementation details. Strategies may or may not change over time, which may
cause new test failures, presumably due to the discovery of new bugs due to a
new kind of witness being generated. These sorts of changes may happen in
semver compatible releases.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [quickcheck](https://docs.rs/macro.quickcheck.html)
- A macro for writing quickcheck tests.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Gen](https://docs.rs/struct.Gen.html)
- `Gen`represents a PRNG.
- [NoShrink](https://docs.rs/struct.NoShrink.html)
- Wrapper for disabling shrinking for an Arbitrary
- [Quick](https://docs.rs/struct.QuickCheck.html)- Check
- The main `QuickCheck`type for setting configuration and running`QuickCheck`.
- [Test](https://docs.rs/struct.TestResult.html)- Result
- Describes the status of a single instance of a test.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Arbitrary](https://docs.rs/trait.Arbitrary.html)
- `Arbitrary`describes types whose values can be randomly generated and shrunk.
- [Testable](https://docs.rs/trait.Testable.html)
- `Testable`describes types (e.g., a function) whose values can be tested.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [empty_](https://docs.rs/fn.empty_shrinker.html)- shrinker
- Creates a shrinker with zero elements.
- [quickcheck](https://docs.rs/fn.quickcheck.html)
- Convenience function for running `QuickCheck`.
- [single_](https://docs.rs/fn.single_shrinker.html)- shrinker
- Creates a shrinker with a single element.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# rsomics_average_degree_connectivity - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rsomics-average-degree-connectivity/0.1.1/rsomics_average_degree_connectivity/

## Expand description

Average degree connectivity (Pastor-Satorras k_nn) — value-exact port of
`networkx.average_degree_connectivity`.

For an undirected unweighted graph, the average degree connectivity maps a
degree `k` to the average degree of the nearest neighbours of the nodes of
degree `k`. Following networkx, it is computed as the accumulation

```
dsum[k]  += sum(deg(w) for w in neighbours(v))      for every node v of degree k
dnorm[k] += deg(v)
result[k] = dsum[k] / dnorm[k]
```
A self-loop on `v` counts twice toward `deg(v)` (as in networkx), but `v`
appears exactly once in `neighbours(v)` — so it contributes `deg(v)` once to
its own dsum term. `dnorm[k] = k * count(k)`, so the k=0 class (isolated
nodes) would divide by zero; networkx returns `dsum[0]` verbatim there.
Edge-list input cannot introduce a degree-0 node, so that branch is
unreachable here.

Barrat, Barthélemy, Pastor-Satorras & Vespignani, “The architecture of complex weighted networks”, PNAS 101(11):3747-3752 (2004).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Average](https://docs.rs/struct.AverageDegreeConnectivity.html)- Degree - Connectivity
- Result payload: the `k -> value`map serialised as an object under`by_degree`.
- [Connectivity](https://docs.rs/struct.Connectivity.html)
- One `degree -> average neighbour degree`row, sorted by ascending degree.
- [Graph](https://docs.rs/struct.Graph.html)
- Undirected simple graph over interned integer node ids.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [average_](https://docs.rs/fn.average_degree_connectivity.html)- degree_ - connectivity
- Compute the average degree connectivity, replicating networkx’s dsum/dnorm accumulation so the division structure — and thus the f64 result — matches value-exactly.
- [average_](https://docs.rs/fn.average_degree_connectivity_from_edge_list.html)- degree_ - connectivity_ - from_ - edge_ - list
- Parse an edge list and compute the average degree connectivity in one call.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_edge_list.html)- edge_ - list
- Parse a whitespace-delimited `u v`edge list.`#`comments and blank lines are skipped. Parallel edges are deduplicated and self-loops kept once in the adjacency, matching the`nx.Graph`that`nx.parse_edgelist`builds. A kept self-loop appears a single time in`adj[v]`; its double contribution to`deg(v)`is added in`average_degree_connectivity`.

# durability - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/durability/0.6.12/durability/

## Expand description

`durability`: crash-consistent persistence primitives.

Scope:

- directory abstraction (`Directory`)
- on-disk framing constants (`formats`)
- append-only record log (`recordlog`)
- generic write-ahead log (`walog`)
- CRC-validated checkpoint snapshots (`checkpoint`)
- generic recovery (`recover::recover_with_wal`) and segment-specific recovery (`recover`,`publish`) with the default`postcard`feature

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- `postcard`(default): serde/postcard typed WAL, checkpoint, recovery, and publish helpers.
- `async`: tokio-compatible async directory abstraction.
- `mmap`: mmap and advisory helpers.

With `default-features = false`, the crate still provides the directory abstraction,
raw record logs, raw checkpoint payloads, WAL framing/maintenance, and sync helpers.

[§](https://docs.rs#contract-what-you-can-rely-on)Contract (what you can rely on)

This crate is designed around two different “strength levels”:

- **Crash-consistent + integrity-checked**(default)- Detects corruption (CRC/magic/version/type mismatches) and errors loudly.
- Supports best-effort recovery of a **torn tail**(partial record write) in the**final**log segment.
- Guarantees a **prefix property**under best-effort replay: recovered operations are a prefix of the successfully written operation stream (no garbage / no reordering).

- **Stable-storage durability**(opt-in)- Requires explicit barriers (`fsync`/`sync_all`) and sometimes**parent directory sync**.
- Use `storage::sync_file``storage::sync_parent_dir``flush_and_sync()`helpers where you need “survives power loss after success” semantics.

- Requires explicit barriers (

Terminology:

- `flush()`is a- **visibility boundary**, not a stable-storage guarantee.
- “Best-effort” is intentionally narrow; it never masks corruption.

Note: this crate intentionally exposes *traits and framing*.
Higher-level crates generally decide directory layout, naming, and lifecycle policies,
but some primitives (notably `walog`) assume a conventional `wal/` directory.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use error::`- [PersistenceError](https://docs.rs/error/enum.PersistenceError.html);
- `pub use error::`- [PersistenceResult](https://docs.rs/error/type.PersistenceResult.html);
- `pub use storage::`- [Directory](https://docs.rs/storage/trait.Directory.html);
- `pub use storage::`- [FsDirectory](https://docs.rs/storage/struct.FsDirectory.html);
- `pub use storage::`- [MemoryDirectory](https://docs.rs/storage/struct.MemoryDirectory.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [async_](https://docs.rs/async_dir/index.html)- dir
- Async directory trait and blocking adapter.
- [checkpoint](https://docs.rs/checkpoint/index.html)
- Generic checkpoint file (single snapshot blob).
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Error types for `durability`.
- [mmap](https://docs.rs/mmap/index.html)
- Memory-mapped file access with advisory hints.
- [publish](https://docs.rs/publish/index.html)
- Crash-safe checkpoint publishing and WAL truncation helpers.
- [recordlog](https://docs.rs/recordlog/index.html)
- Append-only record log (generic WAL primitive).
- [recover](https://docs.rs/recover/index.html)
- Crash recovery using checkpoint + WAL replay.
- [storage](https://docs.rs/storage/index.html)
- Storage abstraction for durability.
- [walog](https://docs.rs/walog/index.html)
- Write-ahead log (WAL) for incremental updates.

# rsomics_average_neighbor_degree - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rsomics-average-neighbor-degree/0.1.1/rsomics_average_neighbor_degree/

## Expand description

Average neighbor degree — value-exact port of `networkx.average_neighbor_degree`.

For each node v: `sum(degree(w) for w in neighbors(v)) / degree(v)`.
Isolated nodes (degree 0) get 0.0.

Nodes are interned to integer indices for O(m) cache-friendly computation.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Graph](https://docs.rs/struct.Graph.html)
- Parsed graph: intern table + integer adjacency.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [average_](https://docs.rs/fn.average_neighbor_degree.html)- neighbor_ - degree
- Compute average neighbor degree for every node.
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_edgelist.html)- edgelist
- Parse an edge-list from text (whitespace-delimited `u v`lines). Lines starting with`#`and blank lines are skipped.

# rustld - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rustld/0.1.56/rustld/

## Expand description

Rustld is a modern (and working) ELF x86_64 & aarch64 loader (static & dynamic linker + compatible glibc & musl) written in Rust
You can run (almost) **everything** with it.

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-sdk)Rust SDK:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
// With syscall trampoline obfuscation:
rustld::ElfLoader::new_with_obf(true).execute_from_bytes(target_bytes, target_argv, None, None, false);
// Without obfuscation:
rustld::ElfLoader::new().execute_from_bytes(target_bytes, target_argv, None, None, false);
// Optional explicit entrypoint:
rustld::ElfLoader::new_with_obf(true).execute_from_bytes_with_entry(
    target_bytes, target_argv,
    Some("hello"), // or None
    None,          // or Some(0x399)
    None, None, false,
);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#basic-usage-example)Basic usage example:

```
use std::{ffi::OsStr, os::fd::AsRawFd, os::unix::ffi::OsStrExt};
use rustld::ElfLoader;
fn main() {
    unsafe {
        let argv_storage = collect_process_arguments();
        if argv_storage.len() < 2 {
            eprintln!(
                "Usage: rustld [--entry-symbol <name> | --entry-addr <addr>] <program> [args...]"
            );
            std::process::exit(1);
        }
        let mut args = argv_storage.into_iter();
        let _self_name = args.next();
        let mut entry_symbol: Option<String> = None;
        let mut entry_address: Option<usize> = None;
        let mut target_argv: Vec<String> = Vec::new();
        while let Some(arg) = args.next() {
            if arg == "--entry-symbol" {
                let Some(symbol) = args.next() else {
                    eprintln!("Error: --entry-symbol expects a value");
                    std::process::exit(1);
                };
                entry_symbol = Some(symbol);
                continue;
            }
            if arg == "--entry-addr" {
                let Some(raw_addr) = args.next() else {
                    eprintln!("Error: --entry-addr expects a value");
                    std::process::exit(1);
                };
                let parsed = parse_address(&raw_addr);
                entry_address = Some(parsed);
                continue;
            }
            target_argv.push(arg);
            target_argv.extend(args);
            break;
        }
        if target_argv.is_empty() {
            eprintln!("Error: missing target program path");
            std::process::exit(1);
        }
        if entry_symbol.is_some() && entry_address.is_some() {
            eprintln!("Error: --entry-symbol and --entry-addr are mutually exclusive");
            std::process::exit(1);
        }
        let target_bytes = map_file_readonly(OsStr::from_bytes(target_argv[0].as_bytes()));
        #[cfg(debug_assertions)]
        eprintln!("Executing target binary: {}", target_argv[0]);
        if entry_symbol.is_some() || entry_address.is_some() {
            ElfLoader::new_with_obf(true).execute_from_bytes_with_entry(
                target_bytes,
                target_argv,
                entry_symbol.as_deref(),
                entry_address,
                None,
                None,
                false,
            );
        } else {
            ElfLoader::new_with_obf(true).execute_from_bytes(target_bytes, target_argv, None, None, false);
        }
    }
}
fn parse_address(raw: &str) -> usize {
    let (digits, radix) = if let Some(hex) = raw.strip_prefix("0x") {
        (hex, 16)
    } else if let Some(hex) = raw.strip_prefix("0X") {
        (hex, 16)
    } else {
        (raw, 10)
    };
    match usize::from_str_radix(digits, radix) {
        Ok(value) => value,
        Err(_) => {
            eprintln!("Error: invalid entry address: {raw}");
            std::process::exit(1);
        }
    }
}
fn collect_process_arguments() -> Vec<String> {
    std::env::args_os()
        .map(|arg| arg.to_string_lossy().into_owned())
        .collect()
}
unsafe fn map_file_readonly(path: &OsStr) -> &'static [u8] {
    use rustld::syscall::mmap::{self, MAP_PRIVATE, PROT_READ};
    let file = match std::fs::File::open(path) {
        Ok(file) => file,
        Err(error) => {
            eprintln!("Error: could not open target binary: {error}");
            std::process::exit(1);
        }
    };
    let length = match file.metadata() {
        Ok(metadata) => metadata.len() as usize,
        Err(error) => {
            eprintln!("Error: could not stat target binary: {error}");
            std::process::exit(1);
        }
    };
    if length == 0 {
        eprintln!("Error: target binary is empty");
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
    let mapped = mmap::mmap(
        core::ptr::null_mut(),
        length,
        PROT_READ,
        MAP_PRIVATE,
        file.as_raw_fd() as isize,
        0,
    );
    let mapped_addr = mapped as isize;
    if mapped_addr < 0 {
        eprintln!("Error: could not map target binary");
        std::process::exit(1);
    }
    core::mem::drop(file);
    core::slice::from_raw_parts(mapped as *const u8, length)
}
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use runtime_loader::`- [host_environment_pointer](https://docs.rs/runtime_loader/fn.host_environment_pointer.html);
- `pub use runtime_loader::`- [ElfLoader](https://docs.rs/runtime_loader/struct.ElfLoader.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- An item in the auxiliary vector.
- [Auxiliary](https://docs.rs/struct.AuxiliaryVectorIter.html)- Vector - Iter
- An iterator over a `AT_NULL`terminated list of auxiliary vector items.

# posthog_rs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/posthog-rs/0.17.1/posthog_rs/

## Expand description

Official Rust SDK for PostHog.

Use [ client](https://docs.rs/fn.client.html) to construct a

[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html)

`Client`[to capture analytics events, and](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html)

`Event`[with](https://docs.rs/struct.Client.html#method.evaluate_flags)

`Client::evaluate_flags`[for feature flag evaluation.](https://docs.rs/struct.EvaluateFlagsOptions.html)

`EvaluateFlagsOptions`See the [PostHog Rust SDK documentation](https://posthog.com/docs/libraries/rust)
for installation, configuration, and more examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

Add `posthog-rs` to your `Cargo.toml`, then initialize a client with your
project API key.

```
use posthog_rs::{client, EvaluateFlagsOptions, Event};
#[cfg(feature = "async-client")]
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), posthog_rs::Error> {
    let api_key = std::env::var("POSTHOG_API_KEY")
        .expect("set POSTHOG_API_KEY to your PostHog project API key");
    let posthog = client(api_key.as_str()).await;
    let distinct_id = "user-123";
    // Capture an analytics event.
    let mut event = Event::new("signed_up", distinct_id);
    event.insert_prop("plan", "pro")?;
    posthog.capture(event);
    // Evaluate feature flags once, then read from the snapshot.
    let flags = posthog
        .evaluate_flags(distinct_id, EvaluateFlagsOptions::default())
        .await?;
    if flags.is_enabled("new-onboarding") {
        let mut event = Event::new("onboarding_step_completed", distinct_id);
        event.with_flags(&flags.only_accessed());
        posthog.capture(event);
    }
    Ok(())
}
#[cfg(not(feature = "async-client"))]
fn main() -> Result<(), posthog_rs::Error> {
    let api_key = std::env::var("POSTHOG_API_KEY")
        .expect("set POSTHOG_API_KEY to your PostHog project API key");
    let posthog = client(api_key.as_str());
    let distinct_id = "user-123";
    // Capture an analytics event.
    let mut event = Event::new("signed_up", distinct_id);
    event.insert_prop("plan", "pro")?;
    posthog.capture(event);
    // Evaluate feature flags once, then read from the snapshot.
    let flags = posthog.evaluate_flags(distinct_id, EvaluateFlagsOptions::default())?;
    if flags.is_enabled("new-onboarding") {
        let mut event = Event::new("onboarding_step_completed", distinct_id);
        event.with_flags(&flags.only_accessed());
        posthog.capture(event);
    }
    Ok(())
}
```

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Capture](https://docs.rs/enum.CaptureCompression.html)- Compression
- Request-body compression algorithm for the capture pipelines.
- [Client](https://docs.rs/enum.ClientOptionsBuilderError.html)- Options - Builder - Error
- Error type for ClientOptionsBuilder
- [Endpoint](https://docs.rs/enum.Endpoint.html)
- API endpoints used by the SDK for different operations.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- Errors that can occur when using the PostHog client.
- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.ErrorTrackingOptionsBuilderError.html)- Tracking - Options - Builder - Error
- Error type for ErrorTrackingOptionsBuilder
- [Feature](https://docs.rs/enum.FeatureFlagsResponse.html)- Flags - Response
- Response from the PostHog feature flags API.
- [Flag](https://docs.rs/enum.FlagValue.html)- Value
- The value of a feature flag evaluation.
- [Post](https://docs.rs/enum.PostHogError.html)- HogError
- A terminal failure on one of the SDK’s network surfaces, passed by reference
to each registered `on_error`hook.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_HOST.html)- HOST
- Default host (US by default)
- [EU_](https://docs.rs/constant.EU_INGESTION_ENDPOINT.html)- INGESTION_ - ENDPOINT
- EU ingestion endpoint
- [US_](https://docs.rs/constant.US_INGESTION_ENDPOINT.html)- INGESTION_ - ENDPOINT
- US ingestion endpoint

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [capture](https://docs.rs/fn.capture.html)
- Capture the provided event using the global client.
- [capture_](https://docs.rs/fn.capture_exception.html)- exception
- Capture a Rust error personlessly using the global client.
- [capture_](https://docs.rs/fn.capture_exception_with.html)- exception_ - with
- Capture a Rust error with optional context using the global client.
- [client](https://docs.rs/fn.client.html)
- Construct an async PostHog client from an API key or `ClientOptions`
- [disable_](https://docs.rs/fn.disable_global.html)- global
- Prevent the global client from being initialized.
- [flush](https://docs.rs/fn.flush.html)
- Flush the global client’s queued events, awaiting the worker’s next delivery
attempt. No-op if `init_global`has not run.
- [global_](https://docs.rs/fn.global_is_disabled.html)- is_ - disabled
- Return `true`if global client initialization has been disabled.
- [init_](https://docs.rs/fn.init_global.html)- global
- Initialize the global client singleton.
- [match_](https://docs.rs/fn.match_feature_flag.html)- feature_ - flag
- Evaluate a feature flag definition against person and optional group context.
- [match_](https://docs.rs/fn.match_feature_flag_with_context.html)- feature_ - flag_ - with_ - context
- Match a feature flag with full context (cohorts, other flags).
- [match_](https://docs.rs/fn.match_property_with_context.html)- property_ - with_ - context
- Match a property with additional context for cohorts and flag dependencies.
- [shutdown](https://docs.rs/fn.shutdown.html)
- Flush and stop the global client’s background worker. Idempotent; no-op if
`init_global`has not run.

# ferridriver - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ferridriver/0.5.0/ferridriver/

## Expand description

ferridriver – Rust-based browser automation library.

Provides a Playwright-shaped API for browser automation across
multiple backends (CDP WebSocket, CDP Pipes, Playwright `WebKit`,
`WebDriver` `BiDi`).

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use ferridriver::{chromium, Page};
use ferridriver::options::{LaunchOptions, RoleOptions};
let browser = chromium().launch(LaunchOptions::default()).await?;
let page = browser.new_page_with_url("https://example.com").await?;
// Playwright-style locators
page.get_by_role("link", &RoleOptions { name: Some("More".into()), ..Default::default() })
    .click(None).await?;
// Content extraction
let title = page.title().await?;
let md = page.markdown().await?;
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [actions](https://docs.rs/actions/index.html)
- Core automation primitives – shared by MCP tools, BDD steps, and library consumers.
- [backend](https://docs.rs/backend/index.html)
- Backend abstraction layer for browser automation.
- [browser](https://docs.rs/browser/index.html)
- Browser management – mirrors Playwright’s `Browser`interface.
- [browser_](https://docs.rs/browser_type/index.html)- type
- `BrowserType`— Playwright-shaped factory for launching and connecting to browsers.
- [codegen](https://docs.rs/codegen/index.html)
- Interactive code recorder (codegen).
- [console_](https://docs.rs/console_message/index.html)- message
- `ConsoleMessage`— live handle for page-side- `console.*`calls.
- [context](https://docs.rs/context/index.html)
- `BrowserContext`– isolated browser environment with pages, cookies, and logs.
- [dialog](https://docs.rs/dialog/index.html)
- `Dialog`— live handle for JavaScript dialogs (- `alert`,- `confirm`,- `prompt`,- `beforeunload`).
- [disposable](https://docs.rs/disposable/index.html)
- Playwright parity: `client/disposable.ts``Disposable`/`DisposableStub`.
- [download](https://docs.rs/download/index.html)
- `Download`— live handle for browser-initiated downloads intercepted via CDP- `Browser.downloadWillBegin`+- `Browser.downloadProgress`or- `BiDi`- `browsingContext.downloadWillBegin`+- `browsingContext.downloadEnd`.
- [element_](https://docs.rs/element_handle/index.html)- handle
- `ElementHandle`—- `JSHandle`specialisation for DOM elements.
- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- Structured error taxonomy for ferridriver’s public API.
- [events](https://docs.rs/events/index.html)
- Event system for Page, Frame, and `BrowserContext`.
- [ffmpeg](https://docs.rs/ffmpeg/index.html)
- Video encoding via ffmpeg subprocess (matches Playwright’s approach).
- [file_](https://docs.rs/file_chooser/index.html)- chooser
- `FileChooser`— live handle for- `<input type=file>`file pickers intercepted via- `Page.fileChooserOpened`(CDP) /- `input.fileDialogOpened`(- `BiDi`).
- [frame](https://docs.rs/frame/index.html)
- Frame API – mirrors Playwright’s Frame interface.
- [har](https://docs.rs/har/index.html)
- HAR (HTTP Archive) replay for `page.routeFromHAR`/`context.routeFromHAR`.
- [http_](https://docs.rs/http_client/index.html)- client
- WHATWG-fetch-compatible HTTP client – the runner-side request
stack, separate from the browser/page network. Backs both the
`fetch`global and the Playwright-style`request`binding.
- [install](https://docs.rs/install/index.html)
- Browser installation module.
- [js_](https://docs.rs/js_handle/index.html)- handle
- `JSHandle`— lifecycle object for an arbitrary JavaScript value in the page.
- [locator](https://docs.rs/locator/index.html)
- Lazy element locator.
- [locator_](https://docs.rs/locator_handler/index.html)- handler
- Locator handler registry — Playwright’s `addLocatorHandler`/`removeLocatorHandler`.
- [network](https://docs.rs/network/index.html)
- Network lifecycle objects: `Request`,`Response`,`WebSocket`.
- [observed](https://docs.rs/observed/index.html)
- Per-page console / page-error retention backing
`page.consoleMessages()`/`page.pageErrors()`(Playwright parity).
- [options](https://docs.rs/options/index.html)
- Option structs for the Page and Locator API.
- [page](https://docs.rs/page/index.html)
- High-level Page API – mirrors Playwright’s Page interface.
- [protocol](https://docs.rs/protocol/index.html)
- Wire-level protocol types shared with Playwright.
- [route](https://docs.rs/route/index.html)
- Network request interception – `page.route()`/`page.unroute()`.
- [selectors](https://docs.rs/selectors/index.html)
- Playwright-style selector engine.
- [snapshot](https://docs.rs/snapshot/index.html)
- Accessibility tree snapshot — compact, LLM-friendly format.
- [state](https://docs.rs/state/index.html)
- Browser state management with instance→context→page hierarchy.
- [steps](https://docs.rs/steps/index.html)
- BDD step definitions — trait-based registry with self-documenting steps.
- [tracing](https://docs.rs/tracing/index.html)
- `Tracing`— the- `context.tracing.*`surface.
- [url_](https://docs.rs/url_matcher/index.html)- matcher
- Playwright-compatible URL matching.
- [video](https://docs.rs/video/index.html)
- Video recording via CDP screencast + in-process ffmpeg encoding.
- [web_](https://docs.rs/web_error/index.html)- error
- `WebError`— live handle for page-side unhandled errors and unhandled promise rejections.
- [web_](https://docs.rs/web_socket_route/index.html)- socket_ - route
- `WebSocketRoute`— page-side WebSocket interception (- `page.routeWebSocket`/- `context.routeWebSocket`, Playwright 1.60).

# sim_lib_music_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-music-core/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_music_core/

## Expand description

Core music model layer for the SIM music constellation.

SIM is a Rust runtime with multiple codec surfaces; this crate supplies the concrete music domain that those surfaces operate on. It defines the music object model (notes, chords, melodies, scores), the descriptor metadata that describes music components and their ports and parameters, events and lanes, the piano roll and time grid, players and playables, performances and takes, the arranger, freeze surfaces, traces, the component registry, and the citizen integration that registers these types with the runtime.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Arranger](https://docs.rs/struct.Arranger.html)
- Arrangement of playable material laid out across lanes on a timeline.
- [Arranger](https://docs.rs/struct.ArrangerDiagnostic.html)- Diagnostic
- Diagnostic raised while rendering a placement.
- [Arranger](https://docs.rs/struct.ArrangerPlacement.html)- Placement
- Single placement of playable material at a point on the arranger timeline.
- [Arranger](https://docs.rs/struct.ArrangerRender.html)- Render
- Result of rendering an [Arranger](https://docs.rs/struct.Arranger.html): play events plus diagnostics.
- [Audio](https://docs.rs/struct.AudioEvent.html)- Event
- An audio-frame event covering a span of frames.
- [Automation](https://docs.rs/struct.AutomationCell.html)- Cell
- An automation breakpoint targeting a named parameter.
- [Chain](https://docs.rs/struct.ChainDevice.html)- Device
- A single processing stage in a player chain.
- [Chain](https://docs.rs/struct.ChainPlacement.html)- Placement
- Placement of a chain device: where it runs and under what rate profile.
- [Chain](https://docs.rs/struct.ChainPlacementPlan.html)- Placement - Plan
- Plan listing the placement of every device in a chain.
- [Chain](https://docs.rs/struct.ChainRender.html)- Render
- Result of rendering a chain: the output events and their trace records.
- [Chain](https://docs.rs/struct.ChainTraceRecord.html)- Trace - Record
- A single trace record describing one action in a player chain.
- [Channel](https://docs.rs/struct.Channel.html)
- A MIDI channel number in the range `0..=15`.
- [Channel](https://docs.rs/struct.ChannelPressureCell.html)- Pressure - Cell
- A MIDI channel-pressure (aftertouch) cell.
- [Chord](https://docs.rs/struct.Chord.html)
- A set of pitches sounded together, optionally tagged with a chord symbol.
- [Control](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlChangeCell.html)- Change - Cell
- A MIDI control-change cell.
- [Control](https://docs.rs/struct.ControlEvent.html)- Event
- A control-change event setting a named control to a value.
- [Counterpoint](https://docs.rs/struct.Counterpoint.html)
- Several independent melodic lines sounding together with labels.
- [Diagnostic](https://docs.rs/struct.DiagnosticEvent.html)- Event
- A diagnostic message emitted on a lane.
- [Direct](https://docs.rs/struct.DirectRecording.html)- Recording
- A directly captured render: metadata plus its events and traces.
- [Drum](https://docs.rs/struct.DrumCell.html)- Cell
- A drum hit cell addressed by MIDI key.
- [Filter](https://docs.rs/struct.FilterRef.html)- Ref
- Lane filter that keeps a placement only when its lane is retained.
- [Freeze](https://docs.rs/struct.FreezeMeta.html)- Meta
- Reproducibility metadata for a frozen player chain.
- [Frozen](https://docs.rs/struct.FrozenPlayable.html)- Playable
- Fully rendered snapshot of a `Playable`
- [Frozen](https://docs.rs/struct.FrozenPlayerChain.html)- Player - Chain
- A frozen player chain: cached render output keyed by its `FreezeMeta`
- [Held](https://docs.rs/struct.HeldPerformanceNote.html)- Performance - Note
- A note currently held down at a source.
- [Lane](https://docs.rs/struct.LaneDescriptor.html)- Descriptor
- Describes a single lane: its identity, content kind, target, and order.
- [LaneId](https://docs.rs/struct.LaneId.html)
- Stable string identifier for a lane.
- [Melody](https://docs.rs/struct.Melody.html)
- A single monophonic line of notes and rests in sequence.
- [Memory](https://docs.rs/struct.MemoryPerformanceSource.html)- Performance - Source
- An in-memory `PerformanceSource`
- [Midi](https://docs.rs/struct.MidiEvent.html)- Event
- A timestamped MIDI event with provenance.
- [Midi](https://docs.rs/struct.MidiFileObj.html)- File - Obj
- A complete Standard MIDI File wrapped as a music object.
- [Midi](https://docs.rs/struct.MidiPlayEvent.html)- Play - Event
- A raw MIDI event bound to a lane.
- [Midi](https://docs.rs/struct.MidiTrackObj.html)- Track - Obj
- A raw MIDI track wrapped as a music object.
- [Music](https://docs.rs/struct.MusicComponentCitizenDescriptor.html)- Component - Citizen - Descriptor
- Runtime citizen wrapper around a `MusicComponentDescriptor`
- [Music](https://docs.rs/struct.MusicComponentDescriptor.html)- Component - Descriptor
- Full description of a music component: its identity, category, capabilities, ports, lanes, parameters, and behavioral contracts.
- [Music](https://docs.rs/struct.MusicComponentRegistry.html)- Component - Registry
- An ordered collection of music components keyed by qualified id.
- [Music](https://docs.rs/struct.MusicComponentRegistryEntry.html)- Component - Registry - Entry
- A single registered music component, wrapping its descriptor.
- [Music](https://docs.rs/struct.MusicParamDescriptor.html)- Param - Descriptor
- Describes a single configurable parameter of a music component.
- [Music](https://docs.rs/struct.MusicPortDescriptor.html)- Port - Descriptor
- Describes a single input or output port of a music component.
- [Note](https://docs.rs/struct.Note.html)
- A single pitched note with timing, dynamics, and articulation.
- [Note](https://docs.rs/struct.NoteEvent.html)- Event
- A pitched note with duration, velocity, and channel.
- [Object](https://docs.rs/struct.ObjectCell.html)- Cell
- A cell that places a named runtime object on a lane.
- [Par](https://docs.rs/struct.Par.html)
- Parallel composition: children that sound simultaneously.
- [Param](https://docs.rs/struct.ParamSnapshot.html)- Snapshot
- Sorted, deduplicated snapshot of named player parameters.
- [Performance](https://docs.rs/struct.PerformanceEvent.html)- Event
- A performance-intent event tying a rendered time back to its input.
- [Performance](https://docs.rs/struct.PerformanceInput.html)- Input
- A raw performance gesture submitted to a source at a given input time.
- [Performance](https://docs.rs/struct.PerformanceInputBinding.html)- Input - Binding
- Binds a named performance input to a lane and channel.
- [Performance](https://docs.rs/struct.PerformanceNoteKey.html)- Note - Key
- Identity key for a held note, combining channel and pitch.
- [Performance](https://docs.rs/struct.PerformanceSourceState.html)- Source - State
- Mutable performance state tracked by a source.
- [Performance](https://docs.rs/struct.PerformanceTake.html)- Take
- A captured recording of performance events with a content-addressed cassette.
- [Piano](https://docs.rs/struct.PianoRoll.html)- Roll
- A piano roll: a set of timed lanes over a shared timing grid.
- [Piano](https://docs.rs/struct.PianoRollLane.html)- Roll - Lane
- A single lane of a piano roll holding cells of one kind.
- [Pitch](https://docs.rs/struct.Pitch.html)
- An octave-aware pitch: a `PitchClass`
- [Pitch](https://docs.rs/struct.PitchBendCell.html)- Bend - Cell
- A MIDI pitch-bend cell.
- [Pitch](https://docs.rs/struct.PitchClass.html)- Class
- A mod-12 pitch class, where `C = 0`and values increase by semitone to`B = 11`.
- [Pitch](https://docs.rs/struct.PitchEvent.html)- Event
- A bare pitch event without duration or velocity.
- [Placed](https://docs.rs/struct.PlacedChainDevice.html)- Chain - Device
- Pairing of a device id with its resolved placement.
- [Play](https://docs.rs/struct.PlayContext.html)- Context
- Rendering context handed to a `Playable`
- [Playable](https://docs.rs/struct.PlayableDescriptor.html)- Descriptor
- Static description of a `Playable`
- [Playable](https://docs.rs/struct.PlayableEvent.html)- Event
- A reference to a named playable to trigger.
- [Playable](https://docs.rs/struct.PlayableShape.html)- Shape
- Shape record describing the playable protocol surface.
- [Player](https://docs.rs/struct.PlayerChain.html)- Chain
- A source music object plus an ordered chain of devices and an output target.
- [Player](https://docs.rs/struct.PlayerDeviceId.html)- Device - Id
- Stable identifier for a device within a player chain.
- [Player](https://docs.rs/struct.PlayerTargetDescriptor.html)- Target - Descriptor
- Descriptor of a chain’s output target and its rate contract.
- [Poly](https://docs.rs/struct.PolyPressureCell.html)- Pressure - Cell
- A MIDI polyphonic key-pressure cell.
- [Progression](https://docs.rs/struct.Progression.html)
- An ordered sequence of chords, optionally in a named key.
- [Rest](https://docs.rs/struct.Rest.html)
- A span of silence.
- [Scale](https://docs.rs/struct.ScaleDegreeCell.html)- Degree - Cell
- A note addressed by scale degree and octave rather than absolute pitch.
- [Scale](https://docs.rs/struct.ScaleLock.html)- Lock
- A set of allowed pitch classes that incoming notes are snapped to.
- [Score](https://docs.rs/struct.Score.html)
- A top-level score: global settings plus a musical body.
- [Seq](https://docs.rs/struct.Seq.html)
- Sequential composition: children that play one after another.
- [SmfFile](https://docs.rs/struct.SmfFile.html)
- A parsed Standard MIDI File: its format, resolution, and tracks.
- [Source](https://docs.rs/struct.SourceRecording.html)- Recording
- Identifying record for a recorded source, without its rendered output.
- [Tempo](https://docs.rs/struct.TempoMapRef.html)- MapRef
- A reference to a tempo map, carrying its id and constant tempo.
- [Tick](https://docs.rs/struct.TickTime.html)- Time
- A point in musical time measured in ticks at a given resolution.
- [Time](https://docs.rs/struct.TimeGrid.html)- Grid
- Timing grid for a piano roll.
- [Time](https://docs.rs/struct.TimeRange.html)- Range
- A half-open span of ticks `[start, end)`.
- [Timed](https://docs.rs/struct.TimedAtom.html)- Atom
- A single flattened atom together with its absolute onset time.
- [Timed](https://docs.rs/struct.TimedNote.html)- Note
- A note placed at an absolute onset time.
- [Trace](https://docs.rs/struct.TraceEvent.html)- Event
- A trace / debugging step marker on a lane.
